rv.q: Yet the cast, particularly the grinning Monaghan, is too distracted by the rat-a-tat period dialogue to create anything darker or slipperier.
With Rope, they have another audacious, stylish, and captivating production.
This incarnation of Rope is a spellbinding and thoughtful entertainment.
This is a striking attempt at pushing a fairly well-known genre piece into more meaningful territory.

Although Greenberg’s adaptation is far from flawless, and Elliott favors shock value over a slow-burn psychological atmosphere, Rope remains a compelling cautionary tale about intellectual arrogance and elitism.
The production by The New Group’s artistic director Scott Elliott is gripping and compelling enough to overcome the new adaptation’s intrusive elements.
With a starry cast, Rope gives new life to the classic murder mystery that inspired Hitchcock's film.
And, try as it might, with a top-notch design team and a solid cast, the New Group production is neither as urbane nor as suspenseful as it wants to be.
In the end, Greenberg deserves credit for trying to unearth the subtexts buried in previous versions, but without real dramatic tension to hold it all together, this Rope goes slack.
Disappointingly, the tension among the story’s several cat-and-mouse games never grows sufficiently taut to grip one’s attention.
I hope Rope has an extended life after its initial run (which has already been extended) because the aura is sexy, the mood is edge-of-your-seat, and the post-theater discussions are lively.
The ensemble is excellent, finding layers of discomfort, vanity, and social calculation beneath the seemingly civilized conversation.
While the dialogue is sharp and the performances are engaging, the twisty, talky narrative is only intermittently spellbinding and tests limits of believability.
But it doesn’t add a lot to the Hitchcock, beyond the in-your-face sexuality and some salty ripostes that the Hays Office would have snipped out.
But this New Group production, under the direction of Scott Elliott, never achieves the compelling creepiness of the material's previous iterations.
But my frustrations with this production are best summed up by saying, “Skip Rope.”
“Rope” represents off-Broadway at its best and for that we can grade it on a curve.
The brittle repartee – reminiscent of smart scripts penned in a wittier age – is thoroughly entertaining.

cn.t: Critics are divided on The New Group's queer-forward "Rope" adaptation—some praise its bold homoerotic explicitness and strong cast, while others find it sacrifices Hitchcock's suspense for shock value.

vr.q: As uneven as the play is and the confusion I did have, I'm really glad I saw this because I thought some of the changes that Gordon Greenberg made were very interesting.
I struggled to get into this, mostly because I found the characters to be somewhere along the spectrum of irritating to utterly despicable
